title: Vyasa sees the hard days coming
hookLine: while the Pandava and Kaurava cousins are still boys, Vyasa sees where the family is heading and sends his mother away; the first power of book three
carry: siddhi: see change fully, and time opens
tomorrow: Krishna and the handful of rice
last: THE BODY CHANGES; THE SEER DOESN'T.

cards: King Pandu has died in the forest, and his five young sons have been brought home to the palace in Hastinapura. The funeral rites are done.
Then Vyasa, the sage who will one day tell this whole story, comes to his mother, Satyavati. He doesn't bring comfort. He brings a warning.
Mother, he says, the happy days are over. Hard times are coming, and they will get worse. This family will destroy itself.
Don't stay to watch it. Go to the forest, and give yourself to yoga.

teach.h: VYASA: KNOWER OF THE THREE TIMES.
teach.b: Satyavati listens. She takes her two daughters-in-law, Ambika and Ambalika, into the forest, and the Mahabharata says they spent the rest of their lives there in austerity and never saw the war.

Vyasa saw where things were heading while the cousins were still boys. Hindus call sages like him trikalajna, knowers of the three times: past, present and future. Patanjali says how such knowing comes.
Sutra 3.16: by samyama on the three transformations, knowledge of past and future. That's yesterday's teaching: everything changes in property, time and condition.
Rest concentration, meditation and absorption fully on how a thing is changing, and its whole arc opens, where it's been and where it's going.
One reading of the story: a small jealousy between cousins, seen all the way through, already holds a war.

The word for a power like this is siddhi, an accomplishment, a perfection, and 3.16 is the first in a long list. The classical commentators take the siddhis as real capacities that come with deep practice.
Some readers take them more inwardly, as pictures of what clear seeing makes possible. Both readings live in the tradition. But look at what Vyasa does with his.
He doesn't announce it or sell it.

teach.h: HE USES IT TO SPARE HIS MOTHER.
teach.b: He uses it to spare his mother. Soon the sutras will add a warning about all the powers, in its place.

teach.h: SEE CHANGE FULLY, AND TIME OPENS.
teach.b: For now, the teaching is this: the sages saw ahead by seeing change clearly, and the best of them used it to care.

It's part of why Hindu families still take big choices to their elders and ask for a blessing before they act. When a grandparent says, I've seen this before, go slowly, that's a small version of Vyasa's seeing.

how: Hindu stories remember sages like Vyasa as knowers of past, present and future, and the siddhis of Yoga Sutras book three are studied in yoga lineages as signs of mastery; teachers often caution students not to make such powers their goal.

o: a vow of silence kept during a long retreat
a magic spell recited to call down a blessing
an accomplishment, a power from deep practice

games.q: the first power — tap the pairs.
p: the past, what has gone by

s: 3.16 says knowing the future comes from luck or fortune-telling
it comes from samyama on the three transformations: seeing change completely.
Vyasa used his foresight to spare his mother the family's ruin
he sent Satyavati to the forest before the war.
everyone in the tradition reads the powers the same way
the classical commentators take them as real capacities; some readers take them more inwardly.

games.q: you've practiced samyama for years, and you start to sense how things will turn out. what's the knowledge built on, in 3.16?
games.why: 3.16: by samyama on the three transformations, knowledge of past and future. the power grows out of understanding change, yesterday's teaching.

practice: Bring to mind one object near you, a mug, a plant, your own hand, and ask quietly where it came from and where it's going: clay, a seed, your parents; shards, compost, age.
No need for answers you can't know; just let it open both ways. Then come back to the breath, which is only now.

wordCard.voice: Siddhi, an accomplishment, a perfection. The first of the powers in book three, from samyama on how a thing changes.

orig.note: Sanskrit atītānāgata-jñāna: knowledge (jñāna) of the past (atīta) and the not-yet-come (anāgata), 3.16.

carryVoice: Your line: siddhi: see change fully, and time opens. Vyasa used it to care. Day four sixty-eight, done.
